title: Chapter 3 — Growth, and Why It Is Fibonacci

slides.narration: Chapter 3: Growth, and Why It Is Fibonacci. The first distinction happened. Now it happens again — and again — and the pattern of growth turns out to be the only one possible.

Once Omega has examined itself, the result can examine itself too. And that result can examine itself. Each new level of examination sees everything below it. The question is: how fast does this grow?

The answer is the Fibonacci sequence. Each number is the sum of the two before it. One plus one is two. One plus two is three. Two plus three is five. The same pattern behind sunflower spirals, nautilus shells, and pine cones.

This is not a choice the framework makes. It is forced by a single rule: no two adjacent positions in the tower can be occupied at the same time. This hard-core constraint — like a rule that says no two people can sit in adjacent seats — forces the growth to follow Fibonacci. No other pattern is consistent.

Sunflowers arrange their seeds in Fibonacci spirals. Pine cones grow in Fibonacci patterns. These are not coincidences — they are consequences of the same hard-core constraint operating in different physical systems. The tower and the sunflower obey the same rule.
